title: Countless favors
hook: if you counted Allah's favors you could not number them (16:18)

segments.voice: Yesterday: yaqin, the certain thing, and a practice kept until it comes.

Surah sixteen is called an-Nahl, the Bee, after a few verses near its middle. But some early scholars gave it another name: the surah of favors. The opening reads like an inventory. Cattle, for warmth, for food, and, the verse adds, for beauty, when you bring them home in the evening and drive them out in the morning. Horses and mules to ride, and as an adornment. Rain to drink, and for the pastures. Stars to steer by at night. The sea, with fresh fish and things to wear. Then, after the list, the surah stops counting.

Verse eighteen, in Pickthall's translation: "And if ye would count the favour of Allah ye cannot reckon it. Lo! Allah is indeed Forgiving, Merciful." The word is ni'mah, a favor, a blessing, a grace. Some commentators point out it's singular. If you tried to count the favor of God, not the favors, you couldn't. Take one: your breath. It depends on lungs, on air, on a planet with the right mix of gases, on the night you slept through without thinking about it once. One favor opens into a thousand. There's an almost identical verse in Surah Ibrahim, from last week, verse thirty-four. Same opening: if you counted God's favor, you couldn't number it. But it ends differently: truly, man is unjust, ungrateful. Here, in an-Nahl, it ends: truly, God is forgiving, merciful. Commentators have long noticed the pair. One verse looks at what people do with the favors: forget them, waste them, take them as owed. The other looks at what God does in return: forgives, and keeps giving anyway. You can't count the favors, or the times they went unthanked, and both verses say so. The surah's list isn't meant to be finished. It's meant to break down. You start counting cattle and rain, and somewhere around the stars, you realize the counting is hopeless. That moment, when the list fails, is the point. Last week: if you give thanks, I will give you more. Today: you couldn't count them if you tried.
screen: `NI'MAH — A FAVOR, A GRACE.` · `SINGULAR: EVEN ONE IS ENDLESS.` · `14:34 — MAN IS UNGRATEFUL.` · `16:18 — GOD FORGIVES.` · then, large: `UNCOUNTABLE.`

segments.voice: Start counting favors, one per breath: your breath itself, the floor holding you, light, water, someone who knows your name. Somewhere along the way you'll lose count; when you do, stop, and just sit inside the part you can't number. If you pray, you can say alhamdulillah there.
Ni'mah. A favor, a blessing, a grace. In 16:18, even one favor of God is too many to count. Today's word.
Your line: uncountable. Even one favor opens into a thousand. That's day four hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Muslims recite 16:18 and 14:34 as reminders of God's favors, and many teachers have students list blessings to see the list break down, answering with alhamdulillah.

original.note: Arabic: a favor, a blessing, a grace; in 16:18, nimat Allah, God's favor.

trapdoor: what you thought: God gives us a lot.
what it means: even one favor of God opens into more than anyone can count, and He keeps giving even when it goes unthanked.
what a scholar hears: 16:18 nearly repeats 14:34 but ends with ghafur rahim instead of zalum kaffar; some early authorities, such as Qatada, called an-Nahl surat an-ni'am.

chat.says: Why does an-Nahl list cattle, rain and stars, then stop counting?
options: Because God's favor can't be counted; the list is meant to break down.
Because the surah only names the favors that matter most to people.
Because the rest of the list was moved to Surah Ibrahim instead.
chat.meaning: 16:18: if you would count the favor of God, you could not reckon it. The list fails on purpose; that's the point.
